speakers.name: Competitor experts (Aionics, SandboxAQ, Citrine x2, Alice)

summary: AlphaSights expert-compiled primer on CuspAI (unverified, built from 1 former, 5 competitor and 3 customer experts plus public sources). CuspAI 2025 revenue est. £7-12m growing 100-150%, 51-200 FTEs, Series B (£300-350m at ~£2bn, Kleiner, Q3 2026). Revenue is 55-65% custom discovery programs (5-15% gross margin, staff-heavy) and 35-45% MIRA platform access (85-90% GM); EBITDA negative in 2025, 20-25% only targeted 2033-36. Only 40-50% of pilots convert to full contracts; 80-85% retention after. Royalties ~1% (platform) and 3-5% (custom) on discovered materials. Closest competitor Orbital Industries wins full-stack buyers; Citrine wins data-infrastructure tenders; Periodic loses to CuspAI where buyers need capacity within 5 years; Radical AI seen as similar tech with less funding.

title: Is this man the future of US manufacturing?
author: Katherine Laidlaw
summary: Profile of Jim Belosic and SendCutSend (Feb 27, 2026, before the round). Belosic taught himself to code, worked as a web designer, ran a B2B SaaS company, and started SendCutSend in 2018 by financing a $750k laser, planning to rent it to hobbyists. The small-shop software he first wrote is now the blueprint for SendCutSend's factories. Three factories (Reno NV, Paris KY, Arlington TX) run 24/7 with a backup for every machine; scouting a fourth site. 30M+ pieces for 300K+ customers; 8M pieces cut last year; ~60% of the Fortune 500 and nine of ten private rocket launch companies are customers. Turnaround about 48 hours design to delivery; fastest job 32 minutes; China lead times two to three weeks; US steel costs roughly 2x China. Recently added CNC machining (lathes, mills).

title: Company Profile: Senra Systems
summary: Trade-press profile (July 2026, exact day not shown) with the most operational detail on Senra. Two facilities totaling ~95,000 sq ft; ~190 employees, expected ~300 by year-end 2026. Sweet spot 100 to 1,000 units per run; growth mostly from existing customers and referrals, no dedicated BD team historically. Amp (Automated Manufacturing Platform) is internal and touches everything except finance: AI reads BOMs from PDF/Excel/PowerPoint/sketches, an API pulls live distributor pricing and lead times, labor estimates are automatic; quote turnaround ~1 day for simple builds with stock, under 2 weeks when supply chain issues arise. Amp generates per-station work instructions, pushes programs to stripping machines (one machine, ~100 strip operations), serves as the QMS logging defects and root causes, tracks cycle times, and reports 99% first-pass yield. Repeat builds: copying a work order takes ~2 seconds. Black calls the approach 'configuration over automation'. CEO Jordan Black: Ford, then SpaceX harness org and avionics manufacturing R&D.

title: Manufacturing Is a Jenga Problem (Annelies Gamble, w/ Google Cloud)
author: Annelies Gamble
summary: Investor (Annelies Gamble) essay series on factory AI. Core claim across pieces: model capability is not the constraint; value requires unified plant data layers, machine-readable context, closed-loop execution and end-to-end workflow change. Notes that even 99% accuracy is too low in manufacturing and top models score 70-90% on controlled simulation benchmarks (Jenga piece). IMTS notes describe shift from text LLM apps to physical AI.
takeaways: Software-first factory AI faces integration/context burden owner-operators avoid (Q3)
excerpt:
Manufacturing Is a Jenga Problem
A conversation with Praveen Rao, Global Director of Manufacturing at Google Cloud, about the architecture of industrial autonomy.
Annelies Gamble
Oct 13, 2026
10
Share
“It’s always harder to solve a Jenga problem than solve a chess problem.” 
Praveen Rao

title: Old factories could fuel Cincinnati's next manufacturing boom (1872 profile)
author: Casey Weldon
summary: Axios profile of 1872 and its Camp Washington plant. CEO Dan Summers (ex-SpaceX) moved to Cincinnati in 2022, toured ~15 properties and picked the former David Hummel site for its ~30,000 sq ft of rectangular production space and nearby rail. The company moved in in April 2026 and was producing by August 2026. Headcount is 18, expected to be 22 by year-end 2026. The $15M seed was led by the O.H.I.O. Fund, which also connected the company to robotics partners. Summers hopes to build a much larger second factory in Southwest or Central Ohio.

key_facts.fact: 18 employees today, expected 22 by year-end 2026
~30,000 sq ft production space in a 123-year-old former stone masonry building
Moved in April 2026, producing by August 2026
key_facts.quote: We moved in here in April, and we were already producing by August

key_facts.fact: Summers toured ~15 local properties before choosing the site; rectangular layout suits an automated line; nearby rail access
Plans a much larger second factory in Southwest or Central Ohio
O.H.I.O. Fund led the $15M seed and connected Summers with robotics partners
Summers moved to Cincinnati in 2022 to be closer to family
Even an autonomous factory needs skilled welders, engineers, technicians
key_facts.quote: Even an autonomous factory needs highly skilled subject-matter experts.

takeaways: Small team (18) and a rehabbed 30k sq ft building: capex-light entry, so the $15M seed is mostly people plus robot cells, not a greenfield plant.
April-to-August move-in-to-production is a real speed signal for plant stand-up, though output volume is unknown.
Factory 2 is aspirational and unfunded; Ohio-anchored investor base suggests the next round may again be regional/state money unless national VCs engage.
No customers, revenue or pricing disclosed three months post-launch.

title: Ex-OpenAI research chief Bob McGrew's Arda raises $232M for US factories
author: Cristian Dina
summary: Arda (Arda Industries) emerged from stealth on 20 Oct 2026 with a $160M Series A at a $1.5B valuation co-led by Altimeter, Accel and Khosla, plus XYZ, 8VC, SV Angel and Felicis; total raised $232M including a $72M seed led by Accel and Founders Fund. Founders: Bob McGrew (ex-OpenAI chief research officer, Palantir), Augustus Odena (chief AI officer, Adept co-founder), Alex Mark (CTO, ex-Palantir) and Jakob Frick (Palantir, SpaceX). The product is an agent that reads CAD and design docs and produces assembly order, work instructions and station layouts for manual lines; robot programming agents are in prototype. Anduril is the first design partner and customer, running Arda inside ArsenalOS, cutting basic work instructions from 10 hours to 15 minutes. Initial markets: defense and the data-center supply chain (transformers, electrical equipment).

key_facts.fact: $160M Series A at $1.5B valuation, co-led by Altimeter, Accel, Khosla; XYZ, 8VC, SV Angel, Felicis participating
$72M seed led by Accel and Founders Fund; total raised $232M
Emerged from stealth 20 Oct 2026 via CNBC exclusive and BusinessWire release
Founded 2025
key_facts.quote: We started Arda in 2025 to speed up American manufacturing.

key_facts.fact: Team: Bob McGrew (OpenAI research lead 2018-2024, CRO; Palantir product/eng first decade; Army Reserve Detachment 201); Augustus Odena, chief AI officer (Adept co-founder, Google Brain, Meta); Alex Mark, CTO (Palantir eng, IRS Direct File); Jakob Frick, co-founder (Palantir, SpaceX)
Anduril = first design partner and customer; Arda runs inside ArsenalOS
key_facts.quote: We would be behind on our production goals without it

key_facts.fact: Anduril result: basic work instructions 10 hrs -> 15 min; complex engineering work up to 30 hrs -> ~2.5 hrs
Product: agent reads CAD/design docs, derives assembly order, writes work instructions, lays out stations; design changes reach floor without stopping production
key_facts.quote: It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers

key_facts.fact: Roadmap: manual lines today; automated reconfigurable lines next; robot-programming agents in prototype
Markets: defense and data-center supply chain first, then consumer electronics, then robotics
Claim: conventional single-station automation programming takes 3-6 months and ~$1M
Vision quote
key_facts.quote: Imagine a fully automated version of Shenzhen in West Texas

takeaways: The Mar 2026 '$70M at $700M' report was superseded: seed was $72M and the Series A is $160M at $1.5B (Oct 2026).

Product today is manufacturing-engineering copilot (CAD to work instructions and station layout), not factory-video control; the video model and robot programming are roadmap. This is an MES/work-instruction wedge, closer to Anduril's ArsenalOS than to Mind Robotics.
Design partner is Anduril, which is also an Isembard customer: Anduril is the demand anchor for both the owner-operator and the software-first sides of the theme.
Still unknown: pricing model, data rights for CAD/floor data, HQ, headcount, website.

title: DoD Office of Strategic Capital and Commerce: $1.4B package for Vulcan Elements and ReElement ($620M OSC loan, $50M CHIPS incentive, $50M equity, warrants) to build 10,000 t/yr US magnet plant
publisher: Mining.com (reporting Department of War and Commerce announcements)
summary: On Nov 3, 2025 the Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital and the Commerce Department announced a $1.4B partnership with Vulcan Elements (North Carolina sintered NdFeB magnets) and ReElement Technologies (rare earth recycling and refining): a $620M OSC direct loan to Vulcan, an $80M OSC loan to ReElement matched by private capital, $50M of CHIPS incentives and $50M of Commerce equity in Vulcan, $550M of private capital, and warrants to the Department of War in both companies. Vulcan will build and operate a 10,000 metric tonne per year magnet facility (site to be announced). Context: Vulcan's Aug 2025 $65M Series A (Altimeter lead) with a 10 t pilot line in Durham and more than $10M of DoD contracts; China produces ~94% of global rare earth magnets and cut off exports in April 2025. The Sept 2026 '$700M conditional loans' item on samsearch appears to re-report this package; DPA Title III is not named.

key_facts.fact: $1.4B total package announced Nov 3, 2025
key_facts.quote: entered a $1.4 billion partnership with the US government to scale a domestic rare earth magnet supply chain

key_facts.fact: $620M OSC direct loan to Vulcan; $80M OSC loan to ReElement (privately matched)
key_facts.quote: $620 million direct loan from the Office of Strategic Capital

key_facts.fact: $50M CHIPS Act incentives + $50M Commerce equity in Vulcan; $550M private capital; DoW warrants in both companies
key_facts.quote: Commerce Department equity in Vulcan: $50 million of equity

key_facts.fact: Target: 10,000 t/yr sintered NdFeB magnet facility, multi-state site search
key_facts.quote: build, commission, and operate a 10,000-metric-tonne-per-year magnet facility

key_facts.fact: Vulcan Series A $65M (Aug 2025), Altimeter lead, One Investment Management; pilot 10 t in Durham NC; >$10M DoD contracts, nine in eight months
key_facts.quote: Vulcan has landed more than $10 million in Defense Department contracts

key_facts.fact: China ~94% of global rare earth magnet supply; export cutoff April 2025
key_facts.quote: China produces 94% of the global rare earth magnet supply and cut off magnet exports in April

key_facts.fact: Aug 2025 Vulcan-ReElement offtake for light and heavy rare earth oxides
key_facts.quote: In August 2025, Vulcan and ReElement announced a commercial-scale offtake agreement

takeaways: This is the template for how the owner-operator model gets financed at the refining/magnet layer: OSC debt plus Commerce equity plus warrants, with private capital (Altimeter) in the stack.
Vulcan went from 10 t pilot (Mar 2025) to a 10,000 t funded plan in eight months on defense demand; speed of qualification is the moat.
For the slide: pair with MP Materials' July 2025 DoD $400M equity deal as the second data point; DPA Title III is not the instrument here, OSC loans are.

title: Section 232 steel, aluminum and copper tariffs: April 2, 2026 proclamation keeps 50% on metal articles, 25% on derivatives, 10% for US-melted inputs (White & Case summary)
summary: The April 2, 2026 proclamation 'Strengthening Actions Taken to Adjust Imports of Aluminum, Steel, and Copper' (effective April 6, 2026) restructures Section 232 metals tariffs: 50% on articles made entirely or almost entirely of steel, aluminum or copper (Annex I-A), 25% on derivatives (Annex I-B), and a reduced 10% rate for products made with US-melted-and-poured steel, US-smelted-and-cast aluminum or copper. Duties now apply to full customs value and do not stack across metals. Steel and aluminum had gone from 25% (March 2025) to 50% in June 2025; the UK keeps 25%/15%. Grid and industrial equipment get a temporary 15% rate to Jan 1, 2028. The derivative inclusions process is terminated. Russia aluminum stays at 200%.

key_facts.fact: Proclamation April 2, 2026; effective April 6, 2026; no in-transit exception
key_facts.quote: Effective for goods entered ... on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT, April 6, 2026

key_facts.fact: Annex I-A 50% on articles entirely or almost entirely steel (ch. 72/73), aluminum (ch. 76), copper (ch. 74)
key_facts.quote: Annex I-A: 50% on articles made entirely or almost entirely of steel, aluminum, or copper

key_facts.fact: Annex I-B 25% on derivatives; 10% if made with US-melted steel / US-smelted aluminum or copper (previously derivatives with US inputs were exempt)
key_facts.quote: Reduced 10% rate for copper articles and derivatives on Annex I-A or I-B made with U.S. metal inputs

key_facts.fact: Steel/aluminum rose from 25% to 50% in June 2025; UK retains 25% (I-A) and 15% (I-B)
key_facts.quote: the increase from 25% to 50% was proclaimed in June 2025

key_facts.fact: Tariff on full customs value, non-stacking across metals; de minimis if metal <15% of weight
key_facts.quote: Tariffs apply to the full customs value of the product

key_facts.fact: Grid/industrial equipment temporary 15% (10% with US inputs) until Jan 1, 2028
key_facts.quote: Reduction expires January 1, 2028

key_facts.fact: Derivative inclusions process terminated; Commerce/USTR may still add products
key_facts.quote: The prior derivative 'inclusions process' for steel, aluminum, and copper is terminated

key_facts.fact: Russian aluminum 200% (Proclamation 10522, Feb 24, 2023); civil aircraft parts excepted for EU/Japan
key_facts.quote: remain subject to a 200% tariff

takeaways: A 50% wall on metal articles and 25% on derivatives, with a 10% carve-out for US-melted inputs, is a direct subsidy to domestic steel/aluminum/copper processing and to fabricators using US-origin metal.
Melt-and-pour provenance reporting creates a data requirement that software-native suppliers (Nox, 1872) can meet more easily than brokers.
Grid equipment relief to 2028 moderates input costs for the AI buildout but expires; watch for 2027 repricing.

title: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 (via Skillings): China ~72% of refined energy minerals, >90% of rare earth refining; $6.5T of downstream output exposed to magnet controls
publisher: Skillings Mining Review (reporting IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026)
author: Charles Pitts
summary: Skillings' July 2026 write-up of the IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 reports that China holds about 72% of the global market for refined energy minerals and above 90% of rare earth refining (60-90% of refining capacity for lithium, cobalt and REEs). The IEA estimates that Chinese export controls on rare earth magnets, if fully enacted, could put about $6.5 trillion of annual downstream production outside China at risk. Planned non-China REE refining reaches only two-thirds of required output by 2035 (33% gap); copper faces a 30% shortfall, lithium 15%, graphite 25%. Critical minerals investment fell ~9% in 2025. Stockpiling the 11 highest-risk materials would cost under $900M a year; tripling REE prices adds ~0.1% to an EV's cost. Secondary source; pull the IEA PDF to confirm the 72% definition.

title: Manufacturing Excellence (Seraph): Made in America — Re:Build Manufacturing co-founder
summary: Manufacturing Excellence (Sereff, Oct 2024) with Miles Arnone, co-founder/CEO of Re:Build Manufacturing (co-founded with ex-Amazon consumer CEO Jeff Wilke). Diagnoses PE-driven offshoring cycle (Rug Doctor: move plants, then engineering; supplier becomes competitor). Re:Build is a ~4-year-old roll-up/build of 13 sites spanning engineering services plus part/system production, started in composites; funded mostly by family offices plus General Catalyst (sole institutional investor, cannot force a sale). Commercial model: proactively passes 70% of cost-savings to customers, keeps 30% - an aerospace customer moved more work to them after an unsolicited 5% price cut. Cross-site collaboration drives wallet share (electronics design -> drone wings -> full drone assembly; "one neck to choke"), incentivized via cost-transfer pricing and company-wide equity. Skeptical of high-abstraction orchestration software from VC-backed e-commerce founders; value is in floor-level process/quoting knowledge. Shifting from 100% M&A (~7x EBITDA) toward 50/50 organic, with dedicated plants for systems like aircraft landing gear.

Higher volume creates incentive to automate; DoD also pursuing high-low mix of cheaper systems. title: Critical Minerals at Venture Scale (Deep Tech Catalyst, Main Sequence)
summary: Deep Tech Catalyst (The Scenarionist) with Jun Ku, principal at Main Sequence (Sydney; >A$1B AUM, 3 funds, 70+ deals since 2017, CSIRO co-founded). Why critical minerals are now venture-investable: new demand (electrification, AI data centers), incumbents and tier-2/3 miners willing to adopt tech, and non-dilutive government capital (US DOE, ARENA) lowering net capital intensity; one-to-one matching is a common starting point but needs project, plan, likely offtake. Value chain: exploration (AI data fusion, kill bad projects sooner), processing/refining (makes stranded assets economic; tailings, bioleaching, recycling), operations (sensors, precision mining). Business models: license (capped upside), tolling (volume-based, often with reagents/ops), JVs, building own plant (rarer given cost of capital), royalties on NSR, and tech-enabled companies buying assets to become operators (the Mariana-type path). Adoption: miners want to be "first to be second"; start pilots with tier-2/3 players. Funding gap at Series B+ ($10M+ checks); exits unproven, no clear comps.
